The Brahmavidyopaniṣad.
Peace: "May He protect us both"—this is the peace mantra.
It is the indication of the Praṇava-Brahman, the secret meaning of the knowledge of Brahman.
Now the Brahmavidyopaniṣad is declared:
By the grace of that Brahmā, of Viṣṇu of wondrous deeds,
Dhruvāgni expounds the secret concerning the knowledge of Brahman.
Regarding that which is called the single-syllable Brahman, "Om," by the exponents of Brahman—
I shall describe its body, its location, and likewise its three times.
In that regard, three gods are proclaimed, as are the three worlds, the three Vedas, and the three fires;
likewise, there are three measures and a half-measure for the three-syllabled Śiva.

I worship the state of Rāmacandra, which is the perfection of the knowledge of destruction— that which has caused one's own ignorance and its entire mass of effects to vanish through the negation of that ignorance by means of knowledge.

Indeed, this *Brahmavidyopaniṣad*, which is a branch of the *Kṛṣṇayajurveda*, unfolds here, revealing the experience of Brahman— the object of knowledge— which consists of the science of the Praṇava and the Haṃsa-mantra, and which culminates in Brahman alone. Of this [Upaniṣad], by way of its brief text:
(p. 250) The commentary begins. Its introductory section and so forth are similar to those of the *Kaṭhavallī* and other texts.

This knowledge (*vidyā*) is praised as being obtainable through the grace of Brahmā and Viṣṇu. The Śruti itself speaks thus to those who lack self-knowledge, beginning with the word "Now" (*atha*). Now, for those who lack self-knowledge...
Immediately after the perfection of the means appropriate for the knowledge of Brahman, this *Brahmavidyopaniṣad* is proclaimed.

How so? It is through the grace of that Brahman—who is the creator and protector of all worlds—and of Viṣṇu, whose wondrous deeds consist of a power exceedingly skillful in accomplishing even the impossible.

That which is the secret of the knowledge of Brahman—because it must be concealed from those who lack qualification; because it is as skillful as a steady fire in reducing to ashes the cotton-mountain of the world, which is distinct from oneself and consists of one's own ignorance and its effects—is correctly declared to be the inward-facing Supreme Self, non-different from that [fire]. What [is this]? || 1 || What?
In response to the inquiry regarding its essential nature: "That state which all the Vedas proclaim, and which all austerities declare."
That goal which those desiring it practice as a life of sacred celibacy (brahmacarya), that I declare to you in brief: it is "Om."
In accordance with such scriptural passages as these, he clarifies the nature of the *praṇava*, which serves as the support for Brahman along with its various modes: "Om. (2-3)
The manifestation of the four measures (mātrās) of the Praṇava is as follows:
the Ṛgveda, the Gārhapatya fire, the Earth, and Brahman itself—these are explained by the exponents of Brahman as the body of the letter A. || 4 ||
The Yajurveda, the intermediate space (antarikṣa), the Dakṣiṇāgni fire,
and the blessed Lord Viṣṇu are proclaimed to be the syllable *U*.
The Sāmaveda, as well as the heavens and the Āhavanīya fire,
and the Supreme Lord God— these are proclaimed as the syllable *M*.
Then, within the solar disc, the letter *A* is situated in the middle of a conch;
the letter *U*, resembling the moon, is established in its center.
The letter *ma*, however, resembles fire, smokeless and like lightning;
likewise, the three measures (*mātrās*) should be known as having the forms of the Moon, the Sun, and Fire. (8)
The crest (śikhā), resembling a lamp, exists above that;
it should be known as the half-measure (ardhamātrā) situated above the Praṇava.
He explains the meaning of the Sūtra with the words "the Ṛgveda," etc.; and "Brahma" means Brahmā.
4–6 || He states the location and color of the letter *a* and the others: "The sun... etc.
7–8 || Having thus elaborated upon the three measures (*mātrā*), he now elaborates upon the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*): "But the crest-lock (*śikhā*)...
Just as the crest of a lamp exists within a lamp, so too does the half-measure exist above the *praṇava*.
This is the meaning. || 9 ||
Through the yoga of Suṣumnā, there occurs the piercing of the channels and the sun; that supreme crest of flame, subtle and resembling a lotus fiber, becomes visible.
That channel, brilliant like the sun, likewise pierces the sun and goes beyond.
Having pierced seventy-two thousand channels at the crown of the head, she who grants boons to all beings stands as if pervading everything. || 11 ||
He describes the nature of the Suṣumnā, the method for the contemplation of the Praṇava,
and the fruit of the knowledge of Brahman as the substratum and support of all those [limbs], beginning with the words "In the lotus" (padme).
Since the Suṣumnā is the solar channel, for one who has departed through its gateway at the crown of the head, into the Brahma-randhra—

The meaning is that for one who performs the contemplation of the target (lakṣya), the piercing of the seventy-two thousand channels and the piercing of the solar orb (sūryamaṇḍala) occur. || 10-11 ||

Through the dissolution of the resonance of the *praṇava*, liberation is attained; just as the ringing of a bronze bell subsides into silence, so too should the *oṃkāra* be employed for the sake of peace by one who desires all things to be tranquilized. (12)
That in which sound dissolves is proclaimed as the Supreme Brahman;
for when the intellect dissolves into Brahman, one becomes fit for immortality. (13)

He says "like the sound of a bell" to show that even for one who does not practice yoga in this way, its fruit can be attained by taking the *praṇava* as a support— just like the final cessation of the sound of a bronze bell that has been refined sixteen times with mercury and gold.

The yogi who performs the recitation of the *praṇava* in this manner— bringing about its dissolution into the sound of the *praṇava* uttered over a duration of sixteen *mātrās*— is such that his intellect (*dhiḥ*), [here used for] the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) with a change of case (the accusative for the nominative), dissolves along with the sound of the *praṇava*. This is that yogi.
It leads to the state of Brahman, which is the foundation of all, to immortality, and to liberation from the delusion of the existence of anything other than oneself. || 13 ||
The definition of the nature of the individual soul (jīva):
Air, fire, and likewise space—this triad is designated as the individual soul.
That soul is called the vital breath (prāṇa), conceived as being a hundredth part of the tip of a hair. 14.
The entire universe is situated in the region of the navel as the pure reality, perfectly stainless;
it shines like the sun with its rays, entirely auspicious.

In order to reveal the Haṃsa-vidyā, he defines the individual soul (jīva) who practices that vidyā as "the wind" (vāyu). He indicates its location as "in the navel. In reality, the Viśva is a portion of Vaiśvānara; when the portions to be abandoned inherent within it have ceased, it is the pure reality (śuddhatattva).
Through the application of the internal organ, they perceive the individual soul (jīva) as the auspicious Self, turned inward. || 15 ||
An examination of the causes of bondage and liberation:
The individual soul (jīva) constantly mutters the letter *sa* and the letter *ha*, which has emerged from the region of the navel and is free from the pervasion of sense objects. (16)
Therefore, one should know this as partless, just as butter [is extracted] from milk;
it is joined with the causal Self through the five breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas). (17)
Endowed with a single *kalā*, it revolves while situated within the heart;
when the *golaka* in the body is struck by the staff of milk. (18)
In this [state], the great bird dwells swiftly and without rest;
as long as the living soul has not ceased its breathing, it remains in a state of partlessness (niṣkalatā). || 19 ||
Having meditated upon the partless [Self] situated in the sky, one is liberated from the bondage of worldly existence;
he who knows the *haṃsa* residing in the heart, accompanied by the sound of the unstruck (*anāhata*).

That which is self-luminous consciousness-bliss is sung as "Haṃsa. This very one is the individual soul (jīva), who, under the guise of inhalation and exhalation, [utters] the syllable "Sa" at the time of departure, free from the pervasion of sense-objects. For this reason, he is devoid of sense-objects.
Therefore, this [Self] is partless. Just as ghee, although distinct from its cause, milk,
in its causal state is nothing but milk itself, so too this living being (jīva), who occupies the place of the ghee, becomes conjoined with the Self, which occupies the place of the milk.

What is the means for achieving the state of becoming one's own cause? To this it is said: "And by the five breath-controls (prāṇāyāmas)—namely, breath-control, withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), concentration (dhāraṇā), meditative absorption (dhyāna), and samādhi. (17)

It possesses four parts through the division into Viśva, Taijasa, Prājña, and Turya. Thus, while situated in the heart, it wanders amidst the calculations of bondage, liberation, and their effects; this is the meaning.
He says, "But the sphere," to show that as long as it does not enter the Brahma-nāḍī, it wanders incessantly in saṃsāra.
When, at that time, the Suṣumnā-golaka— shining at the apex of the Mūlādhāra triangle existing within the gross body— is,
by means of the Prāṇa or by the principle of the Kuṇḍalinī-śakti endowed with enjoyment, like a rod of milk, white like a rod of milk;

As long as it remains unstruck and unassailed, then within this body the great bird, the *haṃsa*, the life-force that is the support of the vital breaths, moves without rest—just as it is—quickly [attaining] that which is to be destroyed by its own knowledge. (p. 254)

Relying upon its own ignorance, it dwells, dwelling; the meaning is that it wanders through the cycle of existence until the dissolution of all things, which lasts until the attainment of self-knowledge. To the question "When does the cessation of that wandering occur?", he says: "As long as... This individual soul (jīva), having grasped the functions of the vital breaths and so forth, remains as long as it has not exhaled after having inhaled.

As long as one becomes free from the activities of the vital breaths and so forth, one attains a state of partlessness (*niṣkalatā*) in the state of non-conceptuality (*nirvikalpa-avasthā*), characterized by the cessation of the operations of all the sense organs. [This state] abides in the space of the heart and is perceived there. || 19 ||

Having meditated upon the partless Self (niṣkala-ātmāna) situated in the sky—due to the absence of the kalās beginning with Prāṇa and ending with Nāman—one is liberated from the bondage of existence; the meaning is that one ceases from saṃsāra and becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done. The knower of the Haṃsa says, "The Haṃsa alone [is the goal]," and thus states: "Anāhata... and so forth.
The meaning is that it is conjoined with the sound of the unstruck (*anāhata*) and is conditioned by the resonance manifested within the heart. || 20 ||
Through the Haṃsa-vidyā alone is the attainment of the Supreme Lord;
having abandoned both exhalation (recaka) and inhalation (pūraka), the wise one remains steady through retention (kumbhaka).
Having balanced the prāṇa and apāna breaths at the bulb of the navel, being composed, and having respectfully drunk the taste of the nectar situated in the head through meditation; 22.
One who should mutter "haṃsa haṃsa" while consecrating with nectar the Great God, who has the form of a lamp and is blazing in the center of the navel; || 23 ||
For such a person, old age, death, disease, and the like do not exist on this earth.
In this manner, one should perform [this practice] day after day for the sake of attaining the sovereign powers (vibhūti) such as atomization (aṇimā).
A person who is constantly devoted to practice attains the state of lordship;
many have reached the eternal state by means of this single path.
In this world, there is no means for attaining eternity other than the *Haṃsa-vidyā*.
He states that one who meditates on the Supreme Lord during the supreme *kumbhaka* alone attains that [eternity], beginning with the verse "recakam" (exhalation).
21–24 || In the *Haṃsavidyāmṛta*, he praises the Vidyā, [stating] that there is no means for liberation other than this Vidyā—beginning with the words "Many... (verse 25). || 25 ||
p. 255) The procedure for devotion to the Guru of the Haṃsa-vidyā:
He who bestows the supreme, purifying Great Vidyā known as Haṃsa. || 26 ||
One should always perform service for him with supreme wisdom;
whatever he says on this earth—whether auspicious, inauspicious, or otherwise—that one must carry out. (27)
The disciple, filled with contentment, should perform that without hesitation;
for by serving the Guru, a person obtains this Haṃsa-vidyā. (28)

Having directly realized the Self by means of the self as the perfectly immovable Brahman, [one abandons] the connections with the body, birth, and so forth, including those associated with caste and stage of life. (29)
A man should discard other Vedic scriptures like the dust at a tree's feet; he should always practice devotion to his guru for the sake of his greatest welfare. (30)
"The Guru alone is Hari manifest, and none other"—thus the Śruti has declared.

Regarding the teacher of the Haṃsa-vidyā as the Lord (Īśvara), the yogi who follows His command, by His grace, determines "I am Brahman non-different from the inner self" (pratyag-abhinnaṃ brahmāsmi). Having abandoned everything other than himself, he should meditate upon the oneness of the Guru and the Deity as long as the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) persist; thus it is said: "He who bestows... (verse 26).

29. "As long as one's limitations persist, so long should one serve the gurus"—in accordance with this Vedic injunction, one should always practice devotion to the guru. 30. "The guru is indeed Ādinārāyaṇa himself"—this is the Śruti;
[it establishes] that the Self is accessible only through the Śruti and the teacher (ācārya).
That which is stated by the Śruti is the ultimate reality;
therefore, there is no doubt about this in its entirety.
In the event of a contradiction with the Śruti, [any other source] would not be authoritative.
It would lead to calamity without a means of valid cognition. || 32 ||

He who resides within the body is to be known as *sakala* (with parts), while he who is devoid of the body is *niṣkala* (without parts). He is accessible through the instruction of a qualified teacher; where else could he possibly abide? (33)
Whoever should utter "Haṃsa, Haṃsa," [realizes that] Haṃsa is Brahmā, Hari, and Śiva;
this is obtained directly from the mouth of the Guru as the all-facing one.
Just as oil resides in sesame seeds and fragrance in a flower, so does that [Self] abide within and without this body of a person. 35.

That which is stated in the Śruti is authoritative; that which is beyond it is non-authoritative. He says, "By the Śruti," [implying] that through the performance of what is authoritative or non-authoritative, one's own welfare or misfortune shall result. (32) Through the union with or separation from a body, there is the state of being with parts (*sakala*) or without parts (*niṣkala*) for that which is without parts.

He states that [the Self] is to be reached through the instruction of the teacher (deśika) in the verse beginning with "situated in the body" (dehastha). The meaning is that although it is all-pervading and partless (niṣkala), it is accessible only through the instruction of one's own teacher (svācārya) and not otherwise. (33) To the question "Who is the teacher?", he says "the Haṃsa," etc. This has already been explained. (34) [He now explains] the nature of the Haṃsa by means of an illustration.
He states its all-pervasiveness with the words "in sesame seeds," etc. (35).
The distinction between the manifest and the unmanifest deity:
Just as someone, having seen an object with a torch in hand, might discard that torch;
so too, having perceived the object of knowledge through knowledge, one should subsequently abandon that knowledge. (36)
One should know that the flower is the *sakala* (with parts) and its fragrance is the *niṣkala* (without parts);
one should know that the tree is the *sakala* and its shadow is the *niṣkala*. || 37 ||
The reality that is both partless and with parts is established everywhere;
likewise, the means is with parts, while the goal is indeed partless. (38)
In the differentiated state, it is entirely differentiated; likewise, in the undifferentiated state, it is undifferentiated.
It is distinguished by being of one measure, two measures, and three measures. (39)
The half-mora is to be known as the supreme (parā); beyond that is the supreme-most (parāt para).
This is recited as the manifest (sakala), consisting of five parts and five deities.
Brahmā resides in the region of the heart; Viṣṇu is situated in the throat;
Rudra is stationed in the middle of the palate; and Maheśvara is located in the forehead. || 41 ||
One should know Acyuta to be at the tip of the nose; at its end, however, is the supreme state.
Because there is nothing higher than the Supreme, such is the definitive conclusion of the scripture. (42)
One should know that [the Lord] transcends the body, twelve finger-breadths from the tip of the nose;
one should recognize Him as being at its end, for the Lord, residing there, pervades all.
To the objection that even upon the attainment of isolation (kaivalya), the knowledge that assists it should not be abandoned, he says: "Like a torch," etc.
36 || He explains the state of being both manifest (sakala) and unmanifest (niṣkala) regarding the visible and the invisible with the words "like a flower" (puṣpavat).
The tree is the foot of one's own ignorance (svāvidyāpāda). Its nature as a tree arises from the felling by one's own knowledge (svajñāna);
and because the Māyā that causes it acts as a coverer, it has the nature of a shadow—this is the meaning. 37 || Thus is the state of being both unmanifest and manifest.

He says that [the Lord] exists everywhere: "He is partless" (*niṣkala*). In the state of one's own ignorance (*svāvidyā*), which is characterized by parts (*kalā*) distinct from oneself, there is the condition of being "with parts" (*sakala*). In the partless (*niṣkala*), which is the locus for the sublation of that [conditioned state], there is the "partless" in relation to the "with parts," being thus defined by its counter-correlative (*sapratiyogika*).

The meaning is that, through the negation of the qualified (saviśeṣa) which pertains to the partless (niṣkala) that arises dependently and possesses a counter-correlative (sapratyogika), the partless Self (niṣkalātman) devoid of a counter-correlative remains as the residue. || 38 ||
He states that the Supreme Brahman is beyond the four measures beginning with 'a' in the verse: "That which consists of a single measure" (39).
In relation to the three measures (mātrās) beginning with the letter *a*, there is the half-measure (*ardhamātrā*).

That which transcends the five Brahmans seated in the five locations, such as the heart and so forth, is indeed the Supreme Brahman; because it is higher than all else, there is nothing higher than that—thus he says, "fivefold" (verse 40–41). [It is] the infallible (*acyuta*).
To Sadāśiva. || 42 ||

(p. 258) He states its transcendence of the body and its all-pervasiveness with the words "deha... etc. One should know that the inner self (pratyagātman), which is the support for the dissolution [of the breath] at that place twelve finger-breadths from the tip of the nose—the locus where the vital breath (prāṇa) dissolves—is beyond the body. That which is devoid of the state of being internal (pratyagbhāva) is the end of that.

One should know the Supreme Self. This very Supreme Self, the Lord, though situated in that state which transcends all, pervades the universe imagined by Himself in the form of the Cosmic Virāj, the individual soul (otṛ), and so forth. || 43 ||
The supreme secrecy of yoga and the fact that it must be imparted only to those of the highest qualification are shown here:
"Even when the mind is directed elsewhere and the eyes are cast elsewhere, the yoga of yogis nevertheless proceeds uninterrupted. (44)
This, however, is the supreme secret; this, however, is the supreme auspiciousness.
There is nothing higher than this, and there is no auspiciousness greater than this. (45)
Having attained the nectar of pure knowledge, which is the definitive teaching on the supreme syllable,
one should strive to grasp that which is more secret than the secret, worthy of being hidden, and to be preserved with great effort.

It must never be given to one who is not a son, nor to one who is not a disciple; it should be given only to one devoted to the guru and the gods, and to one who is constantly intent on devotion. || 47 ||
This scripture must be bestowed; one should not cause it to be given to others.
The giver of this goes to hell and shall never attain success. 48.

He says "the mind also" because the collection of faculties of yogins might suffer a disruption of yoga due to being preoccupied with their respective functions: the mind is cast upon the *nāda* other than its own self,
and likewise the eye is fixed on the tip of the nose, withdrawn from objects such as forms consisting of conceptual construction.

The meaning is that because of the absence of obstacles to yoga both internally and externally, the uninterrupted nature of the yogi’s yoga is appropriate. (44) He says "this" [verse 45] to show that there is no secret other than this which is the primary fruit of yoga: "Having abandoned everything else... (45)
He states that only the knowledge of the supreme syllable (paramākṣara-jñāna) is always to be grasped, beginning with the word "pure" (śuddha).

The knowledge consisting of the determination of the supreme syllable (paramākṣara) should be received and grasped with effort from the mouth of a teacher. That which is thus most secret must be given to one who is a superior candidate;
it must not be given to others. If one were to give it [to such], then the giver would fall into hell.
He says "it might be," and then: "No. (47–48)
Even for one who possesses only scriptural knowledge, there is an absence of the taint of sin or merit:
"Whether he be a householder, a celibate student, a forest-dweller, or a mendicant—wherever he may be situated, the man of knowledge is always a knower of the supreme syllable. (49)
A person attached to sense objects goes to an auspicious state in another body;
yet, through this very knowledge of the scripture, even a human being in any condition whatsoever [attains liberation]. || 50 ||

He states that "the householder" is not tainted by merits or sins such as the killing of a Brahmin or the horse-sacrifice; for anyone who has attained their life's purpose through the knowledge of the mode of livelihood and so forth is not subject to the taint of merit or sin— even if, in appearance, attachment to sense objects is observed.

This one possesses specialized knowledge (saviśeṣajñānī). The meaning is that at the time of the end of his body, because of the scarcity of attachment to sense objects, the attainment of auspiciousness is desired for him. The meaning is that through knowledge produced solely from the scriptures, there is no staining by future merit or demerit. || 49–50 ||
There are three kinds of teachers: the prompter, the awakener, and the supreme one known as the giver of liberation. || 51 ||
Thus, the teacher on this earth should be known as being of three kinds:
the impeller (codaka) who shows the path, and the awakener (bodhaka) who points out the proper place. || 52 ||
The supreme reality, however, is the giver of liberation; by knowing which, one attains immortality. (p.

260) He explains the threefold nature of the teacher according to the distinctions of the *codaka* and so forth, as well as the state of having accomplished all that is to be done through the knowledge of that [reality]—beginning with the verse "the *codaka*": "One should perform the contemplation: 'I am Brahman.'"

The Vedānta is the "impeller" (codaka), for it impels the one ignorant of their own nature toward Brahman by acting as a guide to the path, saying, "That [Brahman] is indeed you; you are indeed That. The teacher is the "awakener" (bodhaka), for he awakens the one ignorant of their own nature by leading them to Brahman. All this is my very own nature; it is me alone.

"Nothing exists apart from Me even in the slightest degree"—by this supreme instruction, He grants liberation from the delusion of anything other than oneself; thus, the Supreme Lord is the "Giver of Liberation" (mokṣada), because His very nature is the Supreme Reality. He is that through the knowledge of whom the seeker of liberation becomes immortal.
The meaning is "the Lord."
O Gautama, listen briefly to the direct worship within the body, which consists of the contemplation of the Praṇava and the Haṃsa. || 53 ||
Having sacrificed with that, the man goes to the eternal, imperishable state;
he himself shall behold within his own body the partless *bindu*.
O child, the knower of the path always perceives the two solstices and the two equinoxes,
having first performed a watch of the night with *recaka*, *pūraka*, and *kumbhaka* breath-control.
Having first uttered both [the names], one should worship them in due order;
beginning with a prostration, yoga, and mudrā, one should perform the worship.
"O child, the eclipse of the sun is known as the direct sacrifice (pratyakṣayajana). What is that direct sacrifice? Listen to this regarding it," he says: "The direct... (verse 53).
When the vital breath (*prāṇa*) enters the seat of Kuṇḍalinī through the *Piṅgalā* [nāḍī], that alone is the solar eclipse; having sacrificed with this, the sage attains the state of Brahman.
He calls this "direct sacrifice" (*pratyakṣayajana*), saying: "by oneself. [This refers to] the *Iḍā* and *Piṅgalā*, or the *Piṅgalā* and *Iḍā*.

The two movements, the northern course (uttarāyaṇa) and the southern course (dakṣiṇāyana), occur [thus]; likewise, when the vital breath (prāṇa) enters the root-support (mūlādhāra) and the head (mūrdhan), then the two equinoxes (viṣuva) occur. (p. 261)

Thus, one who knows the path of the vital breath (prāṇa) shall himself always perceive— and indeed does perceive— the entire bindu, both with parts (sakala) and without parts (niṣkala), within the body during these two equinoxes. O child, at the outset,
one should practice the exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and retention (kumbhaka), either combined or individually, for the duration of one watch (yāma) every day.

Having performed [this], || 54-55 || one should utter both those mantras previously mentioned—"Oṃ" and "Haṃsa"—preceded by a reflection on their meaning. The yoga of salutation (*namaskāra-yoga*) consists of the reflection: "That which is the meaning of the *praṇava* is 'I am He' (*so'haṃ*"); for this is the reflection on identity.

According to the scripture stating, "Because it is the yoga of salutation (namaskāra), one should proclaim the oneness of 'namas'," one who is joined with that yoga of salutation— by means of the *cinmudrā*, or the *śāmbhavī* and *khecarī* mudrās, accompanied by the realization that there is nothing apart from oneself—
should worship the Self in due order and constantly meditate, "I am He."
"One should worship with the sense of 'I am He' (so'ham-bhāva)," according to the scripture; for this alone is to be understood as direct worship (pratyakṣa-yajana).
Through the knowledge obtained from the yoga of the *haṃsa*, one attains *sāyujya*;
it is said that through such knowledge one reaches union, just as water becomes one with water. (57)
These qualities arise for those who have exerted effort on the path of yoga, because by undertaking yoga, one is cast outside of all suffering. (58)
Having constantly practiced yogic meditation, one's consciousness should attain identity with that [object];
through such knowledge, one should utter the supreme *svarūpa*, the *haṃsa* mantra. (59)

Through the knowledge of Brahman, the state of union (*sāyujya*), which is the identity of the inner self and the Supreme, is described by yogis as being like the merging of water into water. Thus, the qualities of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*) proceed. Since one becomes excluded from all suffering through such practice of yoga, therefore, one should always engage in yogic meditation.

The meaning is as follows: having produced the realization of that origin and attained the state of being Brahman alone simultaneously with that knowledge. Whatever manifests internally or externally, all that is indeed the *haṃsa*; there is nothing whatsoever apart from the *haṃsa*—thus the knower is a *paramahaṃsa*.

He says that one becomes the Supreme Self through knowledge: "From knowledge," etc. He who always utters the *haṃsa* mantra as "I am He" (*so'ham*)—by virtue of this knowledge "I am He," [he realizes] that which is the supreme essential nature of the *haṃsa*.
The meaning is that nothing but one's own non-relative self alone remains; that very thing becomes [the reality]. || 59 ||
The Haṃsa is the locus of perception within the bodies of living beings; the Haṃsa resides eternally in the center of the body as the Infallible One.
The Haṃsa alone is the supreme truth, and the Haṃsa alone is reality itself.
Haṃsa alone is the supreme speech; haṃsa alone is indeed the Vedic [truth].
Haṃsa alone is the supreme Rudra; haṃsa alone is the highest of the high.
Standing in the midst of all the gods is Haṃsa alone, the Great Lord (Maheśvara).
From the earth up to Śiva, there are indeed the phonemes beginning with the letter 'A'.
The *kūṭānta* is indeed the *haṃsa*; thus they are established as the *mātṛkā*.

To the question "Where is that perceived?", he says: "of living beings. The meaning is that the *haṃsa*, through constant contemplation, does not fall away from its own measure and is perceived right here in the heart. Of the *haṃsa*...
He declares its universal nature with the words "the *haṃsa* alone," because it is the inner ruler (*antaryāmin*) of each and every sense organ. (60–61)
He states that both the denoted object and the denoting word are indeed the *haṃsa* alone: "Earth, etc. (verse 62).
By the word *kūṭa*, the letter *kṣa* is expressed.
The practice of samādhi must be preceded by the recollection of the measure of the *haṃsa*;
nowhere is it taught that a mantra devoid of the *mātṛkā* should be imparted. (63)
One should visualize the deity, incomparable like the light of a swan, situated in the center;
facing southward, one should form the gesture of knowledge (jñānamudrā).
One should always maintain meditative absorption while recollecting the *haṃsa* mantra—the divine form, peerless and resembling a stainless crystal. (65)
In the central region [of the heart], having realized the supreme *haṃsa*— which is the nature of the *jñānamudrā* and the unity of the *mātṛkā* and the mantra— as the light of the *haṃsa*,
and having bound the *jñānamudrā* while constantly recollecting the mantra of one's own Self, one enters *samādhi*.

He says "one should perform" by means of the word *mātṛkā*. [One should do so] relying upon the incomparable (*anūpamya*), that is, the peerless (*anūpama*, *nirūpama*) deity who faces south among all the gods. Regarding what kind of deity it is, he says *nirmala* (stainless). 63–65.
The determination of the seats of the Haṃsa: the vital airs are prāṇa, apāna, samāna, udāna, and vyāna. (66)
Endowed with the five organs of action and exerting the power of their capacity for action, they are Nāga, Kūrma, Kṛkara, Devadatta, and Dhanañjaya. (67)
Endowed with the five organs of knowledge and exerting the power of wisdom,
the Fire resides in the midst of the power, while the Sun is situated in the navel-cakra.

He by whom the *baddhamudrā* has been formed at the tip of the nose, that is, at his own eyes—[the text] states that the *haṃsa* (the vital breath) resides in the navel-cakra, at the tip of the nose, and in the eyes, asking "Where does the *haṃsa* deserve its seat?"—by the words "prāṇa... [verses 66–67]. [It is situated] between the two powers (*śakti*).

The *haṃsa* itself exists in the form of fire situated in the *mūlādhāra*. The meaning is that by whomsoever the *khecarī-mudrā* has been fixed at the tip of the nose and the two eyes, this very *haṃsa*, having become the sun, is stationed in the *nābhi-cakra*, the tip of the nose, and the two eyes. || 68 ||
Regarding the sequence of practice for the yoga of the swan:
they say that fire resides in the syllable *a*, while [the wind] is situated in the heart at the syllable *u*.
And at the letter *ma*, one should awaken [the energy] between the eyebrows by means of the power of the vital breath (*prāṇaśakti*).
The knot of Brahmā is at the letter *a*, and the knot of Viṣṇu is situated in the heart. (70)
The Rudra-knot between the eyebrows is pierced by the imperishable wind (akṣaravāyu).
Brahmā is established in the syllable *a*, and Viṣṇu resides in the syllable *u*.
Rudra is established in the syllable *ma*; beyond that is the one higher than the highest within it.
By whomsoever the throat is constricted and the channels and so forth are paralyzed through power (*śakti*), [he attains that state]. (72)
When this rasanā is pressed, she ascends upwards through the sixteen [cakras],
reaching the Trikūṭa, the threefold [state], the Golākhya, and likewise the Nikhara.

Moving the Kundalinī, piercing the vital breaths, and breaking through the lunar orb, one reaches the Trishankhu-vajra, which has the syllable Om as its upper stalk and the space between the eyebrows as its opening.
Accomplishing the vajra-pitchers, one should seal the nine gates;
mounted upon the flower and the wind, [the practitioner is] both with passion and likewise devoid of qualities.
In the abode of Brahmā, however, there is the Sound (nāda), which is Śaṅkinī, raining down nectar;
she illuminates the lamp of knowledge that extracts the essence of the circle of the six cakras. 76.
One should constantly worship the Lord who dwells within all beings, the Sovereign of All, beholding Him as one's own self—free from affliction and consisting of pure knowledge. (77)
That which is visible in divine form is all-pervading and stainless;
dwelling within the bodies of living beings, it utters the word "Haṃsa, Haṃsa.
It is the knot of the prāṇa and apāna breaths, and is designated as the "Ajapā" [mantra].
One thousand, two myriads, and six hundred times reciting [this] constantly, the *haṃsa* that has fallen away is designated as "I am He" (*so 'ham*). (79)
A renunciant should always meditate eternally on the lower Liṅga in the eastern part, the western Jyotirliṅga in the Śikhinī [the top of the head], and the [central] Liṅga between the eyebrows.
He states that one should awaken by means of the power of *prāṇa* him who dwells within the triad of *mātrās*—*a*, *u*, and *m*—in the form of Virāṭ and the others:
"The letter *a*... and so forth. They say that the fire Vaiśvānara resides in the letter *a* and in the Mūlādhāra. The remainder is clear. || 69 ||

The three knots that exist within the triad of measures (mātrās) characterized by the forms and so forth of the aforementioned locations are pierced by the wind of the knowledge of dissolution (*haṃsa-jñāna-vāyu*). Thereupon, Brahmā and the others manifest within the letter *A* and the rest. Upon the cessation of the conceptualization of their bodies, the undifferentiated Supreme Self remains as its own pure essence alone.
He says, "It shines forth," namely, Brahman. || 70–71 ||
He teaches yoga as the means for piercing the three knots (*granthi*) through that vision, beginning with the word "the throat":
"By the *jālandhara-bandha*, having constricted the throat, by whichever yogi, established in *siddhāsana*,
[perceives] within the channels and so forth— at the root of the *suṣumnā*— together with the power of *kuṇḍalinī*."
When the vital breaths and the senses have been immobilized, [the tongue] moves upward; according to the Vedic injunction, "Now, as it rises upward, it is the syllable Oṃ," this tongue—
consisting of sixteen parts beginning with the letter *A* and ending with the letter *Ra*,
like the sixteen-syllabled Praṇava— proceeds upward toward the cavity of the uvula.

Being pressed, it attains a state of attenuation and enters the aperture of Brahma (*brahmabila*). Then, that place where the three channels (*nāḍīs*) attain unity is the "Three Peaks" (*trikūṭa*), the middle of the eyebrows;
through its divisions such as the *mūlādhāra* and the *viśuddhi*, it shines forth in a threefold manner. Therein, by the word "cow" (*go*), [the following is meant].

The five elements beginning with earth and their effects are said to be that [unmanifest]; that unmanifest power (*avyakta-śakti*) is this "Golā," wherein [all things] dissolve into their own nature at the time of the final dissolution (*pralaya*). From that which consists of her, the "Golākha" sky—the unevolved space (*avyākṛtākāśa*)—has emerged.

The meaning is that there exists Brahman—the sky of consciousness (cidākāśa), the place of delight for yogis, which is the aggregate of all things from the manifest and unmanifest down to space and earth. Alternatively, by the word "go," the tongue is meant;
and thus it is taught in the Haṭha Tantra: "One should eat cow-flesh."
Because it has been stated in the *Aṃśavivaraṇa* that "the tongue is denoted by the word 'go'," the rest is the same [as previously explained]. || 73 ||
Furthermore, this is a specific qualification of Trikūṭa:

he is called Triśaṅkha because he devours (khādati) the three-fold "triśam"—the threefold pleasure and pain—perceived within his own mind, which arises from desire, aversion, and the desire of others; [this is] by those who are not yogis.

p. 266) Because it is indestructible at all times, it is *vajra*; because it is the locus where the three measures (*mātrā*) beginning with *a* terminate, it is the syllable *oṃ*; the "upward-stalk" is the opening between the eyebrows, the space between the brows. If the yogin wishes to see the *jyotir-liṅga* there, then—
He says that one beholds the lamp of knowledge through means such as the activation of the *śakti*—namely, "the *kuṇḍalī*" (verse 74).
The *sūryojjyāyī*, *śītalyā*, and others are *vajra-kumbhaka*s, because they possess the skill to pierce the three knots (*granthi*). Then he says that the *nāda* manifests: "sumanaḥ.

Because it is pleasing to the mind (*manojñatvāt*), it is mounted upon the wind (*pavana*), and because it has the vital breath (*prāṇa*) as its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), it is with passion (*sarāga*).
Because it is innate, it is likewise devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), since it is untouched by the three qualities beginning with tamas. || 75 ||
The manifestation of the *nāda* occurs in the abode of Brahman, established by the scripture as "the small lotus-dwelling.
It is called *śaṅkinī* because it scatters (*kirati*) auspiciousness (*śam*), that is, nectar; thus it is the lunar digit that showers immortality.
Then the yogi should manifest it in its primordial form; thus he says: "Six," and so forth.

The meaning is that the wise man should illuminate the reality of the inner self (*pratyaktattva*)— which is called the "lamp of knowledge" because it illuminates the functioning of both knowledge and ignorance, and which supports the six-cakra mandala (beginning with the *mūlādhāra*) turned downwards by holding it upwards— as being of that very nature. || 76 || [The word] *pratyañcam*...

He says "all" to indicate that one should meditate [on Him] as being within all. Then he says "Self" to indicate that one should meditate: "I am the Supreme Brahman, non-different from the inner self. (77) That sage who knows that Supreme Self—who is perceived by the wise in His divine form—as non-different from the inner self, is this very one.

Having become all-pervasive and untainted (*nirañjana*), it is indicated that one should utter the sentence "I am He" (*haṃsaḥ so'ham*) by means of the repetition "Haṃsa, Haṃsa. This is the activity of the contemplation of the *haṃsa*.
|| 78 || Regarding the number of repetitions for the *ajapā* [mantra], he says: "A thousand," etc. || 79 || In this manner, by the yogin who is the *haṃsa*...

He states what must be performed daily by the ascetic (yati) in the verse beginning with "pūrva": one should meditate upon the Varāha-tattva as the lower liṅga in the Mūlādhāra-cakra, which is the eastern part of the Suṣumnā, in accordance with the Śruti passage: "In its center is the great fire, whose flames are universal and whose faces are on all sides."

One should meditate on the western Sūtra-liṅga, which is the individual self (pratyagātman), as "I am," within the fire-flame of the Śikhinī situated in the Anāhata [cakra]. Alternatively, the *yati*— one who strives for the attainment of the state of Brahman alone— is a sage (*muni*) who contemplates the eternal, divine light in the center of the Ājñā-cakra between the eyebrows.
The meaning is that one should always meditate upon the sign of Brahman alone, which is without a counterpart, and maintain the continuous realization: "I am That. || 80 ||

p. 267) The yogi of the *haṃsa* should contemplate his own true nature: "I am Acyuta; I am inconceivable; I am beyond reasoning; I am unborn; I am without wound; I am bodiless; I am without limbs; I am fearless. (81)
I am soundless, I am formless, I am touchless, I am non-dual;
I am tasteless, I am odorless, I am beginningless, I am immortal.
I am imperishable, I am signless, I am ageless, I am partless;
I am without breath, I am without speech, I am inconceivable, I am uncreated. || 83 ||
I am the inner controller; I am ungraspable, indefinable, and without characteristics.
I am without lineage, I am bodiless, I am without eyes, and I am without speech.
I am invisible, I am colorless, I am indivisible, I am the marvelous;
I am unheard, I am unseen, I am to be sought after, and I am immortal. || 85 ||
I am without vital breath, without space, and unchanging from fire;
I am without mind, unborn, extremely subtle, and immutable.
I am free from passion (rajas) and free from darkness (tamas); I am without a material being (asattva) and devoid of qualities (aguṇa).
I am without illusion (amāya), my nature is pure experience (anubhavātman), I am non-dual (ananya), and I am beyond the reach of the senses (aviṣaya). || 87 ||
I am non-dual, I am full, I am unassailable, I am without interior;
I am without ears, I am not long, I am unmanifest, and I am free from disease.
I am the mass of non-dual bliss-consciousness, changeless; I am desireless, untainted, a non-doer, and non-dual. || 89 ||
I am devoid of the effects of ignorance; I am beyond the reach of speech and mind;
I am not small; I am free from sorrow; I am free from conceptual construction; I am without flickering.
I am devoid of beginning, middle, and end; I am like the infinite sky.
I am the very form of self-consciousness; I am a solid mass of blissful consciousness.
I am the nature of bliss and nectar; I abide within the Self as the innermost one.
I am one whose desire is the Self; I am the Supreme Self, the Lord beyond the ether.
I am the Lord, I am the one to be praised, I am the Supreme Person;
I am the most excellent, I am the witness, and I am the highest of all. || 93 ||
I alone am the seer; I am the presiding lord over action, the sovereign of the senses;
I dwell within the cave of the heart as the protector; I am the eye of the eye.
I am consciousness-bliss, the cognizer; I am a mass of consciousness, consisting of consciousness.
I am composed of light, the greatest; I am the light of lights. (95)
I am the witness of darkness; I am the fourth beyond the fourth;
I am the divine God, difficult to perceive; I am the eternal one whose nature is seen through meditation.
I am eternal, I am faultless, I am actionless and stainless;
I am pure, free from conceptual construction, ineffable, and immovable.
I am changeless, eternally pure, devoid of qualities, and free from desire;
I am without senses, eternally the "I," independent, and partless.
I am the Puruṣa, the Supreme Self; I am the ancient and the supreme. I am both the higher and the lower, the wise one; I am the cessation of the phenomenal world. || 99 ||
I am the supreme immortal, I am the full, the ancient Lord;
I am the singular consciousness of perfect bliss, I am the single essence of the inner self. (100)
I am wisdom, I am tranquility, I am the light, the Supreme Lord;
when contemplated as one, I am distinct from both duality and non-duality. || 101 ||
I am the Buddha, I am the protector of beings, I am the Blessed One whose form is light; I am Mahādeva, I am the Great One, I am the great object of knowledge, and I am Maheśvara. || 102 ||
I am liberated, I am the all-pervading Lord, I am the most excellent;
I am the all-encompassing Vaiśvānara, I am Vāsudeva, and I am the one with eyes on every side.
I am superior to all, I am pure, I am Viṣṇu, and I am the creator of the universe; I am stainless, I am the radiant seed, I am peaceful, I am eternal, and I am Śiva.
I am the inner self of all beings; I am the eternal.
I am once and for all manifest, eternally established in my own majesty. 105.
I am the innermost of all, self-luminous; I am the sovereign lord of all. I am the abode of all beings, all-pervading, and the self-ruling monarch.
The witness of all, the self of all, dwelling in the cave of the heart of all beings;
manifesting through the qualities of all the senses, yet devoid of all the senses. || 107 ||
I have transcended the three states; I am the benefactor of all.
I am the self that is full of existence, consciousness, and bliss; I am the object of all love.
I am pure existence-consciousness-bliss; I am self-luminous, a mass of consciousness.
I am the true nature of being, the pure reality, the established Self of all. || 109 ||
I am the pure existence that is the substrate of all; I am the remover of all bonds.
I am the devourer of all; I am the seer of all; I am the experiencer of all. (110)
He who knows this in its true essence is indeed called a person (puruṣa).
Thus ends the Upaniṣad.
He states exactly what must be contemplated by the ascetics (*yatins*) with the words beginning "I am Acyuta":

"I am Acyuta" because my nature is immutable; "inconceivable" (*acintya*) because of the absence of mental fluctuations (*cittavṛtti*); "uninferable" (*atarkya*) because of being inexpressible (*anirvācyatva*);
and "unborn" (*aja*) because of the absence of birth and so forth. The three qualifiers beginning with "unwounded" (*avraṇa*) [are as follows]:...

This is for the purpose of negating the three bodies (*śarīra*). I am fearless (*abhaya*), because of the absence of duality, which is the cause of fear. (81) Furthermore: "I am without sound," and so forth. Because of the absence of the five subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the negation of sound and the other [objects] is established for me. I am non-dual (*advaya*), because of the absence of duality. I am beginningless and immortal (*amṛta*).

Because of the absence of origination and dissolution. Furthermore: "I am imperishable," and so forth. I am imperishable because of the absence of a perishable gross body. I am without marks (*aliṅga*) because of being devoid of characteristics. I am undecaying (*ajara*) because of the absence of the six waves of decay and so forth. I am without breath (*aprāṇa*), I am not mute (*amūka*).

Because of the absence of vital breath and the organ of speech; it is uncreated (*akṛta*), because of the absence of a cause for creation. Furthermore: "I am the inner controller" (*antaryāmin*), and so forth. It is the inner controller because it is within all things. It is ungraspable by the sense organs. It is indefinable because its nature is not "this" (*anidam-svarūpa*). It is without characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*), because of the absence of the three types of characteristics.

He is without lineage (*agotra*), because he is devoid of family and clan. He is without eyes (*acakṣuṣka*), because of the absence of the eye of knowledge (*jñānākṣa*). He is without speech (*avāk*), because of the absence of the organ of action (*karmākṣa*). (84) Furthermore: "I am invisible," and so forth. He is invisible (*adreśya*) because of the absence of anything visible. He is colorless (*avarṇa*) because of the absence of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*). He is indivisible (*akhaṇḍa*) because of his perfection.

The term *adbhuta* (the marvelous): although He is His own non-dual self alone, His state as "marvelous" is appropriate because He appears—conforming to the perspective of those ignorant of Himself—as extending from the waking-within-waking state up to the "single flavor of non-conceptual permission.
He is to be sought by seekers of liberation within the Vedāntic scriptures. He is immortal (*amara*).
Because it is eternally real from the perspective of ultimate truth. Furthermore—“not air,” and so forth.
The mention of air, space, and fire is an illustration for water and earth as well. In the term *atejasaḥ*, the genitive case has the sense of the nominative.
It is non-deviating because it is always of a single nature. It is not perceived by the functions of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Unborn (p.

271), because of being unborn; extremely subtle, because of being subtler even than the unmanifest, which is subtler than a single part of a ten-millionth of a hair; changeless, because of the absence of any trace of modification. Furthermore: "dustless," and so forth.

He is devoid of qualities because of the absence of equilibrium among the three *guṇas*; he is without *māyā* because he is free from illusion; he is of the nature of experience because he is accessible through higher knowledge (*vijñāna*); he is non-dual because he is non-different from Brahman; he is not an object because he is devoid of objective referents. He is non-dual because he is without a counter-correlative; he is not incomplete because [he is not limited] by the individual soul (*jīvātman*). || 87 ||

Because of having a limited vision; or else, because of being full everywhere through the nature of Viṣṇu, who is denoted by the syllable *A*; because I am without exterior, being without interiority due to the absence of any conception of "outer" or "inner";
because of being without instruments (of action), because of the absence of measurement, because of being invisible, and because of being without cavities.
The fourfold qualification beginning with "not a hearer" (aśrotrādi) is thus established. Furthermore—regarding the term "non-dual" (advaya):

because its essential nature is perfect bliss and consciousness, it is "desireless" (aniccha). It is "not small" (analpa) because it is unlimited. It is "sorrowless" (aśoka) because it is devoid of egoism (nirahaṃkṛtitvāt). It is "free from conceptual construction" (avikalpa) because it is beyond thought-constructs (nirvikalpatvāt). It is "without blazing" (avijvalan).
Because He is without fire (niragni). || 90 || He is devoid of beginning, middle, and end, because there is an absence of origination, persistence, and dissolution.

He is like space, because He is the sky of consciousness (cidākāśa). || 91 || He is established in Himself, because He abides in His own glory. He is internal, because He is within all. || 92 || He is the Supreme Person (uttamapuruṣa).

Because He is the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) who is free from the reckoning of the perishable and the imperishable—according to the Smṛti: "But the Supreme Person is another, declared to be the Supreme Self"—He is superior to everything. He is the Witness (Upadraṣṭā) because His nature is that of the witness of all. He is the Highest (Uttaratara) because He transcends everything. He is Absolute (Kevala).

Because there is an absence of all distinctions whatsoever; a seer (*kavi*) because of his transcendent vision; the supervisor of actions (*karmādhyakṣa*) because he bestows the fruits of action upon those who act; the lord of the instruments (*karaṇādhipa*) because he takes the form of the directions, the wind, and so forth;
dwelling in the cave (*guhāśaya*) because he is the nature of the witness within all; the protector (*goptā*) because he is Viṣṇu; the eye of the eye.

Because it is the cause for the functioning of the sense organs, such as the eye [it is the "Inner Controller"]. Because it causes that which is insentient to be conscious, it is the "Conscious One" (cetā). It is greater than the earth and other elements. It is the "Light of lights," because it illuminates the sun and other luminaries. || 94-95 ||

I am *dhruva* (fixed) because of my eternity; || 96 || I am *nirañjana* (stainless) because of my non-attachment. || 97–100 || When contemplated as one, I am Brahman, established through the negation of everything else (*sarvāpahnavasiddha*), because I am to be contemplated in a form that is uniquely non-dual and without a counterpart. I am distinct from both relative duality and non-duality.

Because it is of the nature of supreme non-duality (paramādvaita) devoid of any counter-correlate; 101–103. Śiva, because he devours all that is inauspicious (aśiva) as something distinct from himself; 104. He is eternally manifest (sakṛdvibhāta), his light being unobscured; 105.

He is self-ruling (svarāṭ) because He shines by His own nature alone. || 106 || He is the manifestation of the qualities of all the senses, yet He is devoid of all senses; this is the meaning with respect to the perspectives of those who are ignorant of themselves and those who know themselves. || 107 ||
I am beyond the three states, beginning with waking.
(p. 272) He states the fruit of knowledge: "Thus" (evam).
The statements of one's own experience, beginning with "I am Acyuta" and ending with "the witness of all," have for the most part been explained in *Svānubhūtimahāvākyaratnāvalīprabhālocana*.
The word "Upaniṣad" signifies the conclusion of the Upaniṣad on the knowledge of Brahman.
This brief commentary on the Brahmavidyopaniṣad has been written by Upaniṣadbrahmayogin, the disciple of Śrī Vāsudevendra;
this exposition of the present Upaniṣad consists of two hundred and seventy verses.
Thus ends the commentary on the Brahmavidyopaniṣad, completing the fortieth [treatise] in the venerable exposition of the scripture of the one hundred and eight Upaniṣads beginning with the Īśa.
